paper.title: Predicting thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds using ensemble machine learning based on electron configuration
paper.research_summary: This paper proposes an ensemble machine learning framework—Electron Configuration models with Stacked Generalization (ECSG)—to predict the thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds. ECSG integrates three base-level models grounded in distinct domain knowledge: electron configuration (via ECCNN), atomic properties (Magpie), and interatomic interactions (Roost). The framework achieves high predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.988 on JARVIS) and exceptional sample efficiency (requiring only 1/7 the data of existing models). It is validated across multiple databases (MP, OQMD, JARVIS), applied to unknown composition spaces (perovskite halides, Li-containing oxides, transition metal oxides), and demonstrated in two case studies: discovery of 2D wide bandgap semiconductors and double perovskite oxides—both confirmed via first-principles calculations.

tasks.task_name_raw: Predicting thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds
tasks.objective: Accurately predict whether an inorganic compound is thermodynamically stable (i.e., has decomposition energy ΔHd ≤ 0 meV/atom or within relaxed thresholds of 25–40 meV/atom)
constraints: requires only compositional input (chemical formula) for broad applicability; structural input optional for enhanced accuracy
must generalize to unexplored composition space
must handle class imbalance in stability labels
input_requirements: atomic properties (e.g., atomic number, radius, electronegativity)
output_goal: binary classification label: stable vs. unstable
continuous prediction of decomposition energy ΔHd

evidence.text: Machine learning offers a promising avenue for expediting the discovery of new compounds by accurately predicting their thermodynamic stability.

The thermodynamic stability of materials is typically represented by the decomposition energy (ΔHd)6, which is defined as the total energy difference between a given compound and competing compounds in a specific chemical space.
Compounds with a ΔHd below 0 meV/atom were considered stable and are labeled accordingly.

stages.stage_name_raw: Collecting DFT-computed thermodynamic stability data from public materials databases
stages.stage_goal: Acquire large-scale, experimentally validated or DFT-calculated thermodynamic stability labels (ΔHd) for inorganic compounds

evidence.text: In this work, we compared the performance of various models in predicting the stability of inorganic compounds on three large DFT-computed datasets, MP, OQMD, and JARVIS.

Before using these databases, data preprocessing was required. After excluding noble gas and radioactive elements, the MP database contained 85,014 compounds with information on thermodynamic properties such as formation energy.
We extracted thermodynamic stability data for 496 perovskite halides from the literature.

stages.stage_goal: Transform raw chemical formulas into structured inputs suitable for ML models—including element-fraction vectors, statistical atomic features, graph representations, and electron configuration matrices

evidence.text: The input of ECCNN is a matrix with shape of 118 × 168 × 8, which is encoded by the EC of materials.

Magpie incorporates chemical information for each element into its material representations using features such as atomic electronegativity, atomic radii, and elemental group. This results in a total of 132 features, generated using the Matminer62, and the model is trained using XGBoost.
Roost utilizes Matscholar embeddings63 and employs a GAT with three message-passing layers.

stages.stage_name_raw: Assigning stability labels based on DFT-derived decomposition energy thresholds
stages.stage_goal: Generate binary stability labels by computing or retrieving ΔHd and applying domain-appropriate thresholds (0, 25, or 40 meV/atom)

evidence.text: Compounds with a ΔHd below 0 meV/atom were considered stable and are labeled accordingly.

Considering this, along with the potential uncertainties/errors associated with DFT6, we slightly relax the threshold restriction when classifying materials stability. Consequently, we utilize thresholds of 25 meV/atom and 40 meV/atom to assign stability labels in the data set.

stages.stage_name_raw: Training base-level models (ECCNN, Magpie, Roost) and meta-level model (MLR) via stacked generalization
stages.stage_goal: Train three complementary base models on compositional/EC/atomic/graph features, then train a meta-level linear regressor to combine their outputs

evidence.text: We utilized a highly effective ensemble technique called SG to combine the predictions from these individual models for forecasting the thermodynamic stability of materials.
The base-level models include ECCNN, Roost, and Magpie, denoted as f 1, f 2, and f 3. The meta-level model is a multi-response linear regression (MLR), denoted as F.

stages.stage_name_raw: Benchmarking predictive performance using multiple metrics across datasets
stages.stage_goal: Quantitatively assess model accuracy, robustness, and generalizability using AUC, ACC, F1, AUPR, and regression error (MAE for ΔHd)
stage_input: test sets from MP, OQMD, JARVIS, perovskite halides, Li-oxides, transition metal oxides

evidence.text: Experimental results validate the efficacy of our model in accurately predicting the stability of compounds, achieving an Area Under the Curve score of 0.988.
The performance of the ECSG regressor can be found in Supplementary Table 4, where the mean absolute error of ΔHd in the test set is 0.064 eV/atom, surpassing other models in accuracy.
The resulting ensemble model demonstrated an accuracy, f1-score, and AUC score of 0.971, 0.966, and 0.997, respectively.

stages.stage_name_raw: Enumerating candidate compounds in unexplored composition space
stages.stage_goal: Systematically generate vast candidate sets (e.g., >4 million perovskite oxides) by combinatorial enumeration of cation/anion combinations under charge neutrality constraints
stage_input: list of metal elements up to Bi (67 cations)

evidence.text: We constructed the candidate space of perovskites by enumerating all possible ABO3, A2BB′O6, AA′B2O6, and AA′BB′O6 compounds. In this process, we considered all metal elements up to Bi, resulting in a total of 67 different types of cations that could occupy A-sites or B-sites.
After filtering for charge neutrality, 4,524,608 unique compounds remained, forming the candidate composition space.

stages.stage_name_raw: Screening enumerated candidates using ECSG stability predictions
stages.stage_goal: Rank and filter candidate compounds by predicted stability probability to prioritize high-confidence stable materials for validation
stage_output: 35 top-ranked compounds selected for DFT validation

evidence.text: By setting the cutoff probability to 0.5, we identified 1,877,443 perovskite oxides predicted to be stable, substantially narrowing down our search range.
We randomly selected 35 compounds with stability probabilities greater than 90% (63 in total) for first-principles calculations to validate the accuracy of our machine-learning method.

stages.stage_name_raw: Validating predictions via first-principles DFT calculations
stages.stage_goal: Confirm predicted stability by computing formation energies and constructing convex hulls using VASP
stage_input: VASP computational setup (PBE-GGA, 533 eV cutoff, k-point mesh)

evidence.text: The total energy calculations in this study were performed using the DFT framework as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)64,65.

The findings revealed that, out of the 35 compounds, 25 matched our predictions. Using the convex hull of OQMD and JARVIS as references, 26 and 32 materials are stable among these 35 materials, respectively.
